title: People Operations: Hiring, Onboarding, Performance & Manager Guide
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's standard people operations processes for hiring, employee onboarding, performance and feedback cycles, and manager-facing guidance. It is intended for hiring managers, interviewers, people-ops partners, and people managers who run teams. Follow these procedures to ensure a consistent candidate experience, reliable onboarding, and fair performance management.

Sections:
1) Hiring process and interviewer guide
2) New hire onboarding (preboarding, day 1, 30/90-day plans)
3) Performance and feedback cycles (probation, reviews, promotions, calibration)
4) Manager playbook (1:1s, career conversations, PIPs)
5) Templates and related pages / ownership

1) Hiring process (high level)

Purpose: Maintain predictable time-to-hire, high-quality hires, equitable assessment, and a positive candidate experience.

Scope: All roles at Redwood Inference (ICs, managers, leadership). Exceptions must be approved by Head of People Ops.

Process summary (standard requisition to offer):
- Requisition & role definition (owner: hiring manager + People Ops).
  - Create a short role brief (1-paragraph summary) and a 5–7 item skills/experience scorecard.
  - Attach compensation band guidance from People Ops.
- Sourcing & screening (owner: Recruiting).
  - Recruiter performs initial phone screen; shares notes and score vs. scorecard.
- Interview loop design (owner: hiring manager).
  - Typical loop: Recruiter screen -> Hiring manager intro -> Technical/role exercise -> Cross-functional interview(s) -> Final onsite/loop -> Compensation discussion.
- Decision & debrief (owner: hiring manager).
  - Use structured debrief within 48 hours; fill the interview scorecard and create a recommendation.
- Offer & reference/background checks (owner: Recruiting + People Ops).
  - People Ops prepares offer letter, equity, and benefits summary. Conduct background check and reference checks as per local regulations.

Interview scorecard guidance (required):
- Each interviewer must fill a scorecard that maps to the role's competencies. Typical scorecard sections:
  1) Core skills (technical ability, product sense) — rated 1–5
  2) Role fit (scope, seniority, autonomy) — rated 1–5
  3) Culture & team fit (collaboration, communication) — rated 1–5
  4) Risk flags (gaps or concerns) — free text
  5) Recommendation: Strong hire / Hire / No hire / Hire with reservations

Standard interviewer expectations:
- Be on time and prepared (read the candidate's resume and scorecard).
- Ask behaviorally anchored, open-ended questions.
- Avoid salary/compensation discussions unless asked and recommended by Recruiting.
- Evaluate against the scorecard, not based on cultural fit alone.
- Disclose any conflicts of interest to the hiring manager.

Sample technical interview structure (1-hour):
1) 5 minutes: Brief intro and candidate background
2) 40 minutes: Role-specific problem (coding / design / system architecture / case study) with real-world constraints and follow-up questions
3) 10 minutes: Candidate questions, next steps
4) 5 minutes: Fill scorecard

Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) requirements:
- At least one interviewer from a different team or demographic where possible for each finalist loop.
- Hiring managers should work with Recruiting to ensure diverse candidate slates.

2) New hire onboarding

Goal: Ensure new hires reach productivity quickly and feel psychologically safe and informed. The first 90 days are critical.

Preboarding (2 weeks before start):
- People Ops: send welcome email, benefits overview, new hire paperwork, and start-date logistics.
- IT: provision required accounts (Email, Okta, Slack), laptop order with hardware spec, access requests for primary services (internal repos, monitoring dashboards), and access expiration for contractors if relevant.
- Manager: share a tailored day-1 agenda and 30/90-day goals.

Day 1 checklist (first business day):
- Welcome & orientation (People Ops): company mission, values, org chart, policies (security, code of conduct).
- Manager: 1:1 welcome, team introductions, immediate priorities, setup walkthrough.
- IT: confirm device and access functionality.
- Buddy assigned: an experienced peer for shadowing and social orientation.

30/60/90-day plan (example milestones):
- 30 days: orientation complete, first small deliverable shipped, documented learning goals.
- 60 days: ownership of at least one recurring task/feature, initial cross-team relationships established.
- 90 days: full contribution in primary role area, performance checkpoint with manager.

Onboarding documentation & training:
- Provide links to product docs, architecture overviews, codebase tour, and security training.
- Mandatory trainings (must be completed in first 30 days): Security Awareness, Privacy & Data Handling, and Code of Conduct.

Access matrix (summary):
- New IC: email, Slack, internal wiki, dev repo (read/write after probation), CI dashboards (read), observability dashboards (read).
- New manager: above plus people-relevant admin consoles, hiring tracker access, and compensation planning view (restricted).

3) Performance and feedback cycles

High-level cadence:
- Continuous feedback: encouraged via 1:1s and team retrospectives.
- Quarterly check-ins: alignment to team objectives and short-term goals.
- Twice-yearly formal performance reviews: Mid-year and End-of-year cycles with calibration meetings.

Probation & initial performance checkpoint:
- Standard probation period: 90 days for most hires (varies by local law).
- Manager must hold a formal 90-day checkpoint meeting and document outcome: pass, needs follow-up (extend support), or escalate to People Ops for a targeted performance plan.

Performance review workflow (formal cycle):
1) Self-assessment by the employee (structured form).
2) Manager assessment (competencies, accomplishments, growth areas).
3) Peer feedback collected (optional for ICs; required for managers).
4) Calibration meeting across managers to ensure consistency.
5) Compensation and promotion recommendations reviewed by People Ops.
6) Review meeting with employee; documentation stored in HRIS.

Promotion and level change principles:
- Promotions require demonstrated impact, ownership, and often mentorship of others.
- Managers should prepare a promotion packet: evidence of impact, manager justification, peer feedback, and proposed compensation.
- Promotions are reviewed in the calibration window and require People Ops approval for comp changes.

Corrective actions & Performance Improvement Plans (PIPs):
- Use PIPs sparingly and as a formalized, timebound support mechanism.
- Typical PIP steps: documented performance concerns -> 30/60/90 day plan with measurable goals -> weekly manager check-ins -> People Ops oversight -> clear exit criteria.

4) Manager playbook (practical guidance)

Running effective 1:1s:
- Frequency: weekly for ICs; weekly or biweekly for managers depending on seniority and bandwidth.
- Typical agenda: updates (3–5m), blockers (10–15m), career & development (10m), feedback (5–10m), action items/next steps (5m).
- Document outcomes and action items in a shared, private note.

Career conversations and growth plans:
- Have explicit career conversations at least once per quarter.
- Use role-level expectations (found in leveling guides) to set stretch goals.
- Support with learning budgets and mentoring introductions.

Handling performance concerns early:
- Address issues as soon as they surface with clear examples and documented coaching.
- Provide specific, measurable next steps and a timeline.
- Escalate to People Ops if the issue does not improve after documented coaching cycles.

Running team calibration and compensation planning:
- Managers submit compensation recommendations with short justification and supporting evidence to People Ops.
- Calibration meetings are required to avoid drift—People Ops organizes calibration, and managers must attend prepared.

Manager responsibilities checklist:
- Create clear role expectations and onboarding plan for new hires.
- Hold weekly 1:1s and document notes.
- Give timely feedback and recognition.
- Initiate hiring requests with a clear scorecard.
- Participate in calibration and promotion cycles.

Appendix: sample interview questions (role-specific)
- Engineering (backend): Describe a recent system you built to scale to millions of users. What were the trade-offs?
- Product: Walk me through a time you prioritized competing stakeholder requests. How did you decide?
- Sales/GT M: Give an example of a deal that failed. What would you do differently?

End of document.
